extracted.intended_audience: secondary and undergraduate mathematics instructors (and their students) teaching recursion/discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Classroom-tested projects and worksheets for teaching recursion and discrete-math topics (Josephus problem, recurrence relations via trains, codon equivalence classes, Frobenius coin problem). Includes instructor notes, student exercises, solution sketches, and suggested extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use J(n; k) notation for Josephus last survivor
rubrics_metrics.description: The J.n; k/ notation is very handy for describing the last person left in the Josephus game that starts with n people in the circle and eliminates every kth one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: J.7;5/ = 6 (the sixth person around the circle from the starting player). The convention is to count the starting person as the first player around the circle. Use this notation when recording and reasoning about examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply 'using-what-came-before' recursion for Josephus
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the starting player after an elimination to reduce a Josephus game with n people to a smaller instance with n-1 people, thereby using a previously solved case to find the answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In J.12;3/ the first eliminated is person 3 and person 4 becomes the new starting player; since J.11;3/ = 7, the last standing in the original game is person 10. Use this reduction repeatedly to find patterns and compute values without playing the entire game.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill tables and detect pattern in J(n; k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute J.n; k/ for many n (tabulate results) and look for arithmetic/positional patterns as n increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 3 demonstrates tabling J(n;3) for n=3..14 and noticing that for all n≥2, J(n;3) is three more (clockwise) than J(n-1;3). Ask students to explain why this holds in terms of 'using-what-came-before'. Encourage predicting analogous patterns for other k (e.g., k=4: add 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and analyze the special case J(n) for k=2
rubrics_metrics.description: For the skip number 2 variation use J.n/ to denote the last survivor and study how J.n/ relates to J.n-1/ and powers of two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises prompt filling a large table of J(n) and lead to observations: for all n≥2, J(n) is two more (clockwise) than J(n-1); J(n)=1 iff n is a power of 2; describe a formula using the largest power of 2 ≤ n (write n = 2^m + l to derive J(n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce F(n) for next-to-last survivor and relate to J(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Josephus escapes with a friend, define F.n/ as the position of the friend (next-to-last survivor) and analyze its recurrence and relationship to J.n/.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises show patterns for F(n) (e.g., F(n) is two more than F(n-1) for n≥2) and invite investigation of when F(n)=1 and whether there is a direct relationship between J(n) and F(n). Use tables and experiments to detect patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify by playing or using applet; emphasize concrete verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage students to play the Josephus game or use the provided applet to fill tables and verify observed patterns and predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt: 'Finish playing the game to verify that C is the last one standing.' Provide URL to an applet and suggest students use it to explore variations (different k, different labelings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count distinct combinatorial objects explicitly (trains): 'count the number of different trains you can make'
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked how many trains of a given length you can make, count the number of different trains (distinct sequences of car lengths/colors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: length 4 with two length-1 cars and one length-2 car can be made in three different ways. Record trains (drawings or graph paper) or use manipulatives to ensure complete enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use manipulatives and diagrams to model recurrence relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide physical or drawn models (Cuisenaire rods, colored paper, graph paper) to represent trains of different lengths, to make recursion concrete for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes for the instructor: manipulatives force students to build trains rather than merely represent them symbolically; recommended as optional but beneficial. Diagrams illustrate decomposition by last car and support deriving recurrence relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive recurrence relations with initial conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For each train-building scenario, write a recurrence relation tn = combination of previous tj values with explicit initial conditions that count the number of trains of length n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: tn = tn-1 + tn-2 with t1=1, t2=2 (Fibonacci-like); tn = tn-1 + 2 tn-2 with t1=1, t2=3; tn = tn-1 + 2 tn-3 with initial t1=1,t2=1,t3=3; tn = 2 tn-1 + tn-2 with t1=2,t2=5; tn = tn-1 + tn-2 + tn-3 with t1=1,t2=2,t3=4. Show how adding a last car of each allowed length yields the recurrence and initial values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain completeness of counting via constructive decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify that the counting is complete by describing how every object (train) arises from a previous smaller object by adding a final car of allowed lengths/colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example proof: To make a train of length n, add a length-1 car to each length n-1 train or a length-2 car to each length n-2 train; if counts for n-1 and n-2 are correct then all trains of length n are accounted for. Use this to justify recurrence derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and present combinatorial constructions clearly (diagrams/columns/order)
rubrics_metrics.description: When listing all combinatorial objects show a good order for listing and use columns/boxes/diagrams so students and graders can see how constructions were formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet examples show columns where trains ending in a length-1 car are listed first and those ending in length-2 next; boxing indicates how new trains are formed. Encourage use of ellipses and explicit examples to clarify general descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: For codon-class projects: determine equivalence classes (count, sizes, describe)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each specified equivalence relation on codons, determine the number of equivalence classes, the size of each class, and describe the equivalence classes (not necessarily by listing every element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relations include 'same middle base', 'same first two bases', 'same number of A's', 'same number of C's or U's', 'same three bases (multiset)', 'same bases used (set)'. Use counting techniques; provide examples and organize descriptions to justify counts (e.g., counts 4 classes of size 16 for same middle base).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external biological references and define 'close' when comparing to genetic code
rubrics_metrics.description: Research the actual genetic code and compare the 21 classes (amino acids + stop) to the mathematical equivalence relations; the notion of 'close' must be discussed and defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students need a biology/genetics text or internet resource to find the standard genetic code. Instructor note: two interpretations of 'close' are mentioned (number of classes and structural similarity); use this as an opportunity to discuss how to make 'close' precise in modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce definitions and notation for Frobenius coin problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Define representable integers in terms of coin denominations a1,...,ad (nonnegative integer combinations) and define the Frobenius number g(a1,...,ad) as the largest non-representable integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State gcd(a1,...,ad)=1 for nontrivial representability; use coin-exchange language to motivate. This precise definition is required before posing or proving results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove the 2-coin Frobenius formula g(a,b)=ab-a-b and related counting result
rubrics_metrics.description: For d=2 show g(a,b) = ab - a - b and prove Sylvester's theorem that exactly 1/2 (a-1)(b-1) of the integers between 1 and (a-1)(b-1) are non-representable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet outlines proofs using Euclidean algorithm ideas and counting; these problems are suitable for courses covering gcd and the Euclidean algorithm. Provide guided steps and hints in class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generating functions and rational-function representation for representable sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent the set of representable integers by the generating function F(x) = sum_{k representable} x^k and show it can be written as a rational function of the form P(x)/((1-x^{a1})...(1-x^{ad})).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For d=2 one gets an explicit simple form; for d=3 Denham's theorem shows the numerator polynomial has either 4 or 6 terms leading to semi-explicit formulas. Use this for analytic/computational approaches and to explain algorithmic computability for fixed d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match worksheet depth to student background and give instructor timing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Select problems appropriate to students' background: first nine worksheet questions suit courses discussing gcd and Euclidean algorithm; later ones assume knowledge of greatest-integer function and inverses in Z_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes for the instructor: first six problems of the trains project take ~1 hour; projects can be group activities or homework; provide a forum for students to share ideas. For Frobenius material, indicate which sections are elementary and which are more advanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide open-ended extensions and research-project prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer extensions and undergraduate-research-style problems that explore algorithmic approaches, bounds, vector generalizations, special solved cases, and computational experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example projects for Frobenius: find new algorithms for d≥3, improve bounds, study vector generalizations, extend solved special cases (e.g., arithmetic sequences), and explore the generalized Frobenius number g_j. Encourage computational exploration and literature review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage explicit verification and explanation in solutions (not just answers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require students to explain how they obtained answers (e.g., why a recurrence holds, why counting is complete, why classes have given sizes), not only to supply numerical results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solutions provided illustrate explanations: e.g., demonstrating recurrence derivation by showing how to form length-n trains from shorter ones, or explaining why J(n)=1 iff n is power of 2. Use such explanations as grading criteria.
